status_reason: The sources support a single-method shortlist for an aqueous glucose and lactate measurement, but the concentration range, required performance, optical regime and installation point are not yet known, so the choice between Raman and MIR-ATR stays provisional. The premise that a pilot is workable rests on published precedents, and the supplied material does not say what agreement with the laboratory values would establish.

solution_options.fusion_note: Start with one model per method as the baseline, then fuse the synchronised Raman and mid-IR blocks, scaled so that neither method dominates the joined model. The two probes must look at the same measurement point, and the two data streams must be normalised to a common time step before fusion, with each method keeping its own calibration and diagnostics. Keep the fused model only if it beats the best single method on held-out runs or batches.

proposal.what_would_change_it: Answers on the glucose and lactate range, the required accuracy and the medium's optical density could change the choice: a strongly scattering, high-cell-density medium would favour MIR-ATR or the combined option, while a clear, low-scattering medium would bring NIR transmission or reflection back into the shortlist. A strong fluorescence background on real samples would move the choice away from Raman.
proposal.next_step: Run the first feasibility experiment on representative process samples and compare the in-situ predictions with the existing laboratory glucose and lactate values.

brief_answer: Test Raman first as a single in-situ method: it suits an aqueous medium and is reported to give a molecular fingerprint for glucose and lactate. A mid-IR ATR probe is the natural single-method comparison. Still open: the concentration range and required accuracy, the medium's optical behaviour, the probe location, and what counts as agreement with the laboratory values. A combined Raman + ATR model is a later hypothesis only.
